facts.name: Wild Geranium
facts.notes: Tough, long-lived and easy. The deeply cut leaves often turn red-orange in fall.

sources.title: Michigan Wildflower Farm: Dryland species list
sources.note: Michigan seed grower; marks any species that is not native to Michigan.

sources.title: University of Nebraska Extension: Early Summer Maintenance for Perennials
sources.note: Shear perennial salvia, coreopsis, Shasta daisy, columbine, coral bells, hardy geranium and catmint after flowering; many rebloom in 5 to 6 weeks.

sources.title: Penn State Extension: Cutting Down Perennials in the Fall
sources.note: Cut peonies, daylilies, brunnera and speedwell in fall; cut bee balm and garden phlox with powdery mildew and destroy the leaves; rake up hosta leaves (slug eggs); cut yarrow and Shasta daisy flower stalks but keep the base leaves. Leave grasses, Siberian iris, baptisia, sedum, Joe-Pye weed, coneflower, black-eyed Susan and most natives standing; leave marginally hardy anise hyssop tops over winter; tidy hardy geraniums, heucheras, hellebores and moss phlox in spring.

companions.why: Found with Solomon's seal, ferns, mayapple and woodland phlox; combines with celandine poppy, columbine, foamflower and goat's beard.
